1:
The heading fixes the psalm to the sabbath, and the readers dispute which sabbath. Delitzsch records that it was the sabbath psalm of the post-exilic service, sung at the drink-offering of the first daily lamb, and that the Talmud could not settle whether it looks back to the sabbath of creation or forward to the last sabbath of history; he judges the second more correct. Henry reports a Jewish writer who called it a psalm for the age to come, all sabbath, and adds that believers already enjoy the beginning of that everlasting rest. Clarke will not go so far. The title gives no information about time, occasion or author; the tradition that the first man spoke it is an idle conceit; and he prefers a suggestion that Levites composed it near the close of the captivity. He notices too how abruptly the psalm opens, as though the writer broke out from private thanksgiving to say how good the work was.

What the day requires is answered in two keys. Calvin denies the day is holy in the sense of being devoted to idleness: it is holy in separating us from other occupations so that we may meditate on the divine works, our minds being inconstant and apt to wander when distracted. Right observance, he says, does not consist in idleness, as some absurdly imagine, but in the celebration of the divine name. Henry says the same — the sabbath must be a day not only of holy rest but of holy work, its proper work being praise, which the other services must not thrust into a corner. Augustine relocates the question inward. Rest, he says, is from evil works, and a merely bodily observance abstains from good ones, since it is better to plough than to dance; the sabbath God proclaims is in the heart, for many are idle in their limbs while disturbed in conscience. He prefaces this with a warning that no Christian should promise himself the happiness of the world, since God loves whether he caresses or threatens.

On the goodness of thanksgiving there is only competition in stating it. Spurgeon divides it three ways — good ethically, since it is the Lord's right; good emotionally, since it is pleasant to the heart; good practically, since it leads others to the same homage. A sabbath without thanksgiving, he says, is a sabbath profaned; and since nature teaches the form — the birds singing, the brooks warbling — he cannot understand how one body of Christians deprives itself of so natural a part of worship. Henry calls praise the rent we pay our great Lord, so that we are unjust if we withhold it, and work that is its own wages. Over morning and night, Ellicott calls the assignment of lovingkindness to one and faithfulness to the other a result of Hebrew style, though a fitting one: love breaks through the clouds of doubt as morning rises on the night, while thoughts of unerring justice suit the evening. Clarke reads it as a plan for morning and evening prayer: mercy acknowledged for preservation through the night, faithfulness for the promise kept through the day. On the ten-stringed instrument he quotes a fourth-century commentator who allegorised it as worship through the five senses and the five powers of the soul, then draws a historical inference: had instrumental music been used in the church of that day, the writer would surely have said so. The gladness of the fourth verse is variously sourced: Gill offers creation, providence, redemption or the work of grace; Delitzsch distinguishes the word for God's historical rule from the word for the Creator's works, calling the ability to rejoice in either a gift from above; Ellicott, noting that the verse in Latin gave a famous poet an image of delight in natural beauty, insists the reference is to history, not nature.
5:
The exclamation over God's works draws the largest writing. Spurgeon pairs act with plan: some men think but cannot work and others are drudges working without thought, whereas in the Eternal conception and execution go together. Creation is immeasurable and the wisdom in it unsearchable — man is superficial and God inscrutable, man shallow and God deep. Clarke calls the works multitudinous and splendid, and the thoughts the designs from which they were formed, too profound to be fathomed. Ellicott prefers plans to thoughts, Wesley narrows them to God's counsels in governing world and church, and Gill spreads the works across nature, providence and grace.

The drop to the man who cannot see it is deliberate: what a stoop, says Spurgeon, from the saint to the brute, from the worshipper to the boor — the boorish or boarish man being almost the very Hebrew word, and such a man seeing nothing in nature. Whether the two names describe one failure or two divides the readers. Clarke insists they differ: the first has mind, but buried in flesh, while the second has no mind at all and his stupidity is unavoidable — the first being the man who is all flesh, in whom intellect neither works nor exists. Ellicott separates them differently, deriving the first from a root meaning to eat, so that it names the man who lives for his appetites, and the second from a root meaning fat; in the one the moral sense never came into play, in the other it is overgrown by sensuality. Wesley and Gill treat the pair as one type, the man led by sense rather than reason — Gill adding that man, made far above the brute creatures, by sinning became like the beasts that perish, caring no more for an immortal soul than a beast that has none.

The next verse turns the argument, and Ellicott finds the received translation faulty. The Authorised Version, he says, wrongly introduces a second conjunction; the line runs literally that in the springing of the wicked like grass, all the workers of iniquity flourish to be destroyed for ever — the prosperity of an evil class giving an impulse to evil, only that the destruction may be more signal. The others read it as it stands and reach the same result. Delitzsch calls the prosperity of the ungodly a semblance lasting for a time, a historical occurrence repeated down to the present day and to be closed by a decisive judgment. Henry supplies the proverb — the prosperity of fools shall slay them, and sheep designed for slaughter are put into the fattest pasture — and triumphs in their ruin not as the misery of fellow-creatures but as the honour of God's justice. Spurgeon presses the figure: they grow to die and blossom to be blasted, flowering a short space to wither without end. Clarke draws the rule: God's favour is not measured by prosperity, nor his disapproval by adversity.

Then comes the line Spurgeon singles out as the middle verse of the psalm and the great fact the sabbath song exists to illustrate: others rise to fall, but this one is Most High to eternity — the ungodly destroyed for ever, the Holy One reigning for ever. Gill sees the same antithesis in the grammar and adds a corollary: God endures for ever to inflict the punishment, which is why it is everlasting. Clarke keeps it simpler: the wicked brought down, the Lord exalted eternally for his judgments as well as his mercies. Delitzsch reads it as the moment when the oppressed church stands forth vindicated, God being by nature and rule a height for ever. On the doubled cry against the enemies Gill explains that the calls to attention are for our sake, not God's, the repetition being there for certainty; Henry asks who ever hardened his heart against God and prospered.
10:
Nobody knows what animal the horn belongs to. Delitzsch identifies it with the oryx, one-horned according to the ancient authorities, and reads the horn as defensive power and stately grace at once. Ellicott simply prefers buffalo. Clarke offers the oryx or buffalo, then overrules himself for the rhinoceros as the real single-horned creature of Scripture. Spurgeon leaves the species open — some gigantic ox now unknown — keeping only what matters, that among the ancients it was the favourite symbol of unconquerable power. On the oil, Clarke doubts any sacramental reference and thinks of ordinary anointings after bathing; Wesley makes it the anointing customary at joyful solemnities; Spurgeon, recalling that guests were anointed at feasts, makes it fresh outpourings of grace. He marks the contrast the psalm is building: the brutish grow with a vegetable vigour of their own, while the righteous are dealt with by the Lord himself.

The next verse divides them over words not in the Hebrew. Spurgeon objects that the translators' inserted phrase had better have been left out: the psalmist does not say what he will see, and we have no right to fill the blank. Ellicott recasts the line: the eye looked upon insidious foes without fear, the ears listening to their rising up without alarm. Clarke fills it traditionally: the enemies would be destroyed in the psalmist's own lifetime, so that he would witness it or have authentic report.

Then the two trees. Ellicott observes that this is the only place where the palm stands as an emblem of moral rectitude, whereas the cedar had long served as emblem of kingly might; the contrast he finds striking, an age measured in centuries against the brief day of the grass. Spurgeon draws it from the desert: a palm standing erect, all its strength sent upward in one bold column, thriving in drought, is the godly man who lives where all else perishes; and on the summit, unsheltered from the blast, the cedar keeps its verdure. Grass, which makes hay for oxen, is emblem enough for the unregenerate; cedars, which build the temple, are none too good for the heirs of heaven. Clarke turns antiquarian, quoting a traveller who measured a Lebanon cedar at twelve yards in girth and thirty-seven across its boughs, some a thousand years old. Gill keeps to the mechanics — the palm rises against the greatest weight laid on it, its whole force in its top, which being cut off it dies — and notes that though the singular has led some to find Christ here, it is his people who are meant.

Where the trees are planted is also disputed. Gill recalls that the temple had palm trees carved on its walls, and takes the planting as a bringing out of the world into Christ. Delitzsch makes the temple the soil itself — a planting of the Lord for his praise, in sacred ground and air that impart new powers of life. Clarke will have none of it: there is no allusion, he thinks, to trees planted near the tabernacle, and the verse says only that the righteous flourish in God's ordinances as trees in their proper soil. Wesley agrees that the house means the church, of which good men are members. The fruitfulness of old age closes the psalm. Gill notes that other trees cease bearing when old, whereas grace is often in greatest vigour when nature is decayed, naming several who went to the grave like ripe corn. Ellicott gives the literal words — still shall they sprout in hoary age, sappy and green — of the date palm, which bears to the last. Clarke, more soberly, calls it a rare case to find a man in old age full of faith and spiritual activity, and closes where the psalm does: such lives show how faithful God is, doing nothing evil, nothing unwise, nothing unkind.
